summary: The unit is sound and close to the Hebrew, and its rulings follow Ibn Ezra. The main fault is 24:62, where 'came from Beer-lahai-roi' drops the infinitive that Ibn Ezra reads as 'from coming to' and his summary was misdescribed ('its accent agrees'). 24:57 'her own word' is not English. Two grammar notes were wrong (a 'second took' in 24:61; a conjunctive merkha said to divide 24:63). 24:63 לָשׂוּחַ is correctly 'to walk' with prayer recorded; 'meditate' is now added; context for 'thousands of myriads' and the gate is added.

value: רְבָבָה is ten thousand, so 'thousands of myriads' is a very great number, not a count. In the second wish, 'possess the gate' of the haters means to hold their city: the gate was the city's entry, its defence and its seat of judgment. The wording echoes the promise to Abraham in 22:17, where the seed 'shall possess the gate of his enemies'; here the word is 'those who hate him'.
patches.reason: a reader needs the number and the gate; Radak and Rashi both link the verse to 22:17

value: The wayyiqtol chain runs in three parts: Rebekah rises (3rd feminine singular); her maids mount and go (3rd feminine plural); the servant takes her and goes (3rd masculine singular).
The etnaḥta on הָאִישׁ (61.9) divides 'they went after the man' from 'the servant took Rebekah and went'.
The preposition עַל with the camels is 'on'; the English 'mounted the camels' carries that sense in the verb.
The object marker before רִבְקָה marks her as the object of 'took'; the servant is the subject (the verb is masculine singular).
patches.reason: 'the second took': the verse has one 'took'

patches.value: Isaac had come from coming to Beer-lahai-roi, and he was living in the land of the Negeb.
patches.reason: Ibn Ezra, normative, reads מִבּוֹא as the verbal noun, 'came from coming (to) Beer-lahai-roi'; 'from Beer-lahai-roi' drops the infinitive and reads as though he lived there (the point Ramban raises)

value.english: Isaac had come from coming to
in the land of the Negeb.

patches.reason: follows the new English

patches.value: Ibn Ezra lists readings of בא מבוא: that it is a place name, a place called by two names; that some take it as 'from inside' (מבפנים), as they explain 'shutting every house from entering' (Isa 24:10). He prefers the infinitive, the name of the action, and so its sense is 'came from coming (to) Beer-lahai-roi'. The English follows him.
patches.reason: the summary omitted the first reading and invented 'its accent agrees': וכן טעמו means 'and so its sense'

patches.value: infinitive construct of purpose; Ibn Ezra takes 'to walk' (more fully 'to walk among the bushes', ללכת בין השיחים); Rashi's 'to pray' and Sforno's 'pour out his complaint' are recorded in the apparatus
patches.reason: the note dropped Ibn Ezra's 'among the bushes'

value: Purpose: 'went out to walk', the infinitive with ל after the verb of motion.
The time phrase is an infinitive construct of פָּנָה with ל: 'towards evening'.
The wayyiqtols (went out, lifted, saw) give the sequence; then הִנֵּה with a participle gives the sight as a present scene: 'look, camels were coming'.
The etnaḥta on עָרֶב (63.6) divides the verse: going out to walk towards evening, then the seeing. The merkha on וַיֵּצֵא (63.1) is a conjunctive accent and divides nothing.
patches.reason: the merkha is conjunctive and does not divide the verse

value: לָשׂוּחַ: 'to walk' (Ibn Ezra, 'among the bushes'; Radak, 'to stroll among the bushes'; the lexicon 'go, rove about'); 'to pray' (Rashi, as in 'he pours out his complaint'; Targum Onkelos renders לְצַלָּאָה; Sforno, 'pour out his complaint before the Lord'). 'To meditate', the older English rendering, takes the verb as from שִׂיחַ 'musing, complaint', the same word Rashi and Sforno draw on; no commentator in the pack gives it, and the English does not take it.
patches.reason: 'meditate' is a recorded reading; the old note said only that it was absent
